title:
From Microdata to Macro Forecasts: A Comparative Study of
Aggregation Strategies and Benchmark Models in Social
Protection Spending
content: Does access to transaction-level records affect which forecasting method public-finance analysts should choose? To answer this question, we compare four forecasting strategies applied to a short, highly seasonal time series of child-benefit payments: top-down, bottom-up, data-enrichment, and minimum-trace reconciliation. Our application concerns monthly child-benefit expenditure in Republika Srpska (Bosnia and Herzegovina), where we have approximately a hundred observations of total payments, but more than a million observations of individual payments. We also consider four different ways to deal with the recurring near-zero observations typical of administrative payment data. Under an expanding-window design, where each model can only use information available at the time of each forecast origin, exponential smoothing performs best across every treatment, with minimum-trace reconciliation yielding statistically equivalent accuracy. Enrichment with features from microdata offers no advantage when those features must be known in advance, while machine-learning techniques fail to outperform the benchmarks. The choice of treatment for near-zero observations proves as important as the forecasting method itself. Overall, in the presence of strong seasonality and short time-series, widely-used forecasting techniques remain hard to improve upon, and more data only helps if it provides genuinely forward-looking information.
